data.text: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design. Code design in this lifecycle is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.
points: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.
Code design in the interactive system development lifecycle is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

data.text: Designing an immersive experience involves a design-prototype-evaluation cycle to incorporate user requirements. The design process can start from creativity aided by intuition and expertise, or from guidelines that range from generic high-level rules to detailed micro details. Because interface design requires a design language that is generally different from code design, a prototype can be used as a language for expressing design ideas.
points: Designing an immersive experience involves a design-prototype-evaluation cycle to incorporate user requirements.
Design can start from creativity aided by intuition, expertise, experience, and domain knowledge, or from guidelines like checklists and heuristics.
Design guidelines can be generic high-level rules or detailed specific specifications for micro details.
A design language is used to specify interface design, which is generally different from the language used to specify code design.
A prototype can be considered a language for expressing interface and interaction design ideas.

data.text: VR-specific guidelines for minimizing cybersickness are typically for VR or immersive systems and may not apply to AR systems. Generic design guidelines apply to any interactive system including XR, although they are mostly, not fully, applicable. Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are generic GUI rules that can be partly or fully applicable to XR systems.
points: VR-specific guidelines for minimizing cybersickness are typically for VR or immersive systems but may not apply to AR.
Generic design guidelines apply to any interactive system including XR, although they are mostly, not fully, applicable.
Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are generic GUI rules that can be partly or fully applicable to XR systems.

data.text: Strive for consistency in system and interface design by using internal and external consistency. Design for universal usability to support all user categories. Menu-based options may be preferable to hotkeys because they rely on recognition rather than recall.
points: Strive for consistency in system and interface design.
Use internal consistency for tasks and external consistency to match real-world experience.
Design for universal usability to support all user categories.
Menu options rely on recognition while hotkeys rely on recall.

data.text: Users should be provided with informative feedback for every action they perform. Additionally, dialogues should be designed to yield closure by organizing task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts with feedback at the end of each group.
points: Provide informative feedback to users for every action they perform.
Design dialogues to yield closure by organizing tasks into beginning, middle, and end parts with feedback for each group.

data.text: System design should offer error prevention and simple error handling, which includes keeping error rates low by avoiding placing options side by side that could lead to the wrong action. Error messages should be simple and easy to understand to avoid confusing or scaring the user. Additionally, systems should permit easy reversal of actions, ideally by keeping a reversal option available, through undo and redo facilities which are primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.
points: Offer error prevention and simple error handling.
Keep error rates low by avoiding placing options side by side that could lead to the wrong action.
Provide simple, easy-to-understand information instead of complicated error messages.
Permit easy reversal of actions, ideally by keeping a reversal option available.
Use undo and redo facilities, which are primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.

data.text: Keeping users in control requires that users feel in control, perceive state changes, and receive feedback. Because short-term memory is a non-permanent store limited to five to nine chunks of information, designers should reduce short-term memory load by keeping interface information within that range. These generic usability rules can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.
points: Keeping users in control requires that users feel in control, perceive state changes, and receive feedback.
Short-term memory is a non-permanent store used to aid day-to-day activities.
Short-term memory is limited to holding five to nine chunks of information at a time.
Reducing short-term memory load requires keeping interface information between five and nine chunks.
These generic usability rules can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.

data.text: Interaction in non-immersive settings is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture. For immersive virtual reality or mixed reality experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used to design the experience properly and enhance presence. Interaction in these immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control.
points: Non-immersive interaction is similar to familiar touch and gestures.
Immersive experiences use specialized techniques to enhance presence.
Immersive interaction is categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.
